Remembering Dolly Parton

By Kip Mooney • On August 30, 2026 • In Featured, News Featured, News Comments Off on Remembering Dolly Parton
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:44
Instaread

If you didn't regularly tear up during "I Will Always Love You," that seems almost impossible now. Dolly Parton, an icon of entertainment and generosity, has died at the age of 80.

A musician, actor, producer, philanthropist, and entrepreneur, she really was the most beloved figure in the United States. Regardless of age, background, religious views, or taste in music, there really wasn't anyone who didn't love Dolly.

Born dirt poor in rural Tennessee, she began her singing career as a child, eventually becoming one of the best-selling musicians of all time. Anyone who wrote both "I Will Always Love You" and "Jolene" – let alone in such close proximity – would have a hall of fame career. But Dolly kept writing, kept recording, kept trying new things, releasing a double album in 2023 and collaborating with stars like Sabrina Carpenter and Pitbull.

It didn't all work. Her variety show Dolly only lasted one season. After early successes in Hollywood with 9 to 5 and The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, neither Rhinestone nor Straight Talk are fondly remembered. She only made two more films after that: the barely released comedy Frank McKlusky, C.I. and the dueling choirs movie Joyful Noise. But being part of a movie as beloved as Steel Magnolias makes up for a lot.

Parton won 11 Grammys, three Emmys, a National Medal of Arts, and a Kennedy Center Honor (back when those were still handed out). That she didn't win an Oscar for "9 to 5" might be the Academy's single greatest travesty, though she seemed overjoyed when fellow Tennesseans Three 6 Mafia beat her 25 years later.

While she was an incredible talk show guest, what's most remarkable is how Parton actually used her vast fortune to make the world a better place. She founded the Dollywood Foundation to help students in her hometown stay in school. And the group's Imagination Library program sent millions of books to kids for free every single month. She even donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University to help research of Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine. To see a wealthy person doing so much good so often, especially in an age when most people of her status seem to be laser-focused on making as much money as possible, is enough to bring a tear to your eye.

There will never be anyone like Dolly ever again. Some artists will probably eclipse her in record sales, and it's possible a celebrity will take up her mantle and use their fortune to worthy causes. But no one will ever have her combination of warmth, humor, faith, beauty, talent, maturity, and generosity. Luckily, we were alive at the same time to experience some of it.

About Kip Mooney

Like many film critics born during and after the 1980s, my hero is Roger Ebert. The man was already the best critic in the nation when he won the Pulitzer in 1975, but his indomitable spirit during and after his recent battle with cancer keeps me coming back to read not only his reviews but his insightful commentary on the everyday. But enough about a guy you know a lot about. I knew I was going to be a film critic—some would say a snob—in middle school, when I had to voraciously defend my position that The Royal Tenenbaums was only a million times better than Adam Sandler’s remake of Mr. Deeds. From then on, I would seek out Wes Anderson’s films and avoid Sandler’s like the plague. Still, I like to think of myself as a populist, and I’ll be just as likely to see the next superhero movie as the next Sundance sensation. The thing I most deplore in a movie is laziness. I’d much rather see movies with big ambitions try and fail than movies with no ambitions succeed at simply existing. I’m also a big advocate of fun-bad movies like The Room and most of Nicolas Cage’s work. In the past, I’ve written for The Dallas Morning News and the North Texas Daily, which I edited for a semester. I also contributed to Dallas-based Pegasus News, which in the circle of life, is now part of The Dallas Morning News, where I got my big break in 2007. Eventually, I’d love to write and talk about film full-time, but until that’s a viable career option, I work as an auditor for Wells Fargo. I hope to one day meet my hero, go to the Toronto International Film Festival, and compete on Jeopardy. Until then, I’m excited to share my love of film with you.
